parts.label: (a)
hints: Hint 1: Look at Fig. 11.1 and count how many complete sine-wave cycles fit into the 30 ms interval from t = 0 to t = 30 ms.
Hint 2: Find the time for one cycle in seconds, then use the reciprocal relationship between frequency and period to get f in Hz.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Read the period from the graph**
You are sitting with a repeating sine wave, so first find how long one repeat takes. From $t = 0$ to $t = 30 \text{ ms}$ there are exactly two full cycles. That means one cycle lasts $$T = \frac{30 \text{ ms}}{2} = 15 \text{ ms}$$ A good check is to follow a zero-crossing going up, for example near $t \approx 6 \text{ ms}$, to the next identical zero-crossing going up near $t \approx 21 \text{ ms}$. The gap is $15 \text{ ms}$.

Step 2: **Convert to frequency**
Frequency tells you how many cycles per second, so it is the reciprocal of the period. Remember to work in seconds: $$f = \frac{1}{T} = \frac{1}{15 \times 10^{-3}}$$ $$f \approx 66.7 \text{ Hz} \approx 67 \text{ Hz}$$

parts.label: (b)
key_concepts: mean value of sinusoidal alternating current
symmetry of positive and negative half-cycles
hints: Hint 1: Think about the area under the curve above the time axis compared with the area below it over two whole cycles.
parts.proper_answer: Mean current $= 0 \text{ A}$ because positive and negative half-cycles cancel over whole cycles.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Use symmetry over whole cycles**
For an alternating sine wave the current spends just as much time and just as much size positive as negative. Over $t = 0$ to $30 \text{ ms}$ you have exactly two complete cycles, so every positive loop is matched by an equal negative loop. The average, which is the net area divided by time, therefore cancels to $$I_{mean} = 0 \text{ A}$$ This does not mean nothing happens in the resistor, only that the average directed charge flow is zero.

parts.label: (c)
hints: Hint 1: Read the maximum height of the sine wave from the I-axis in Fig. 11.1 - this is the peak current $I_0$.
Hint 2: Recall how the effective heating current for a sine wave is related to the peak value by a square-root factor.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Find the peak current**
The top of each crest in Fig. 11.1 reaches $$I_0 = 0.75 \text{ A}$$ The troughs reach $-0.75 \text{ A}$, confirming the amplitude is $0.75 \text{ A}$.

Step 2: **Convert peak to r.m.s.**
For a sinusoidal current the root-mean-square value, which is the steady d.c. equivalent for heating, is $$I_{r.m.s.} = \frac{I_0}{\sqrt{2}}$$ $$I_{r.m.s.} = \frac{0.75}{\sqrt{2}} \approx 0.53 \text{ A}$$

parts.label: (d)
hints: Hint 1: Heating depends on $I^2$, so the mean current of zero cannot be used - think about which current value correctly represents the heating effect.
Hint 2: Combine the Joule heating power in the $450 \Omega$ resistor with the total time interval of 30 ms to get energy.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Choose the correct formula for heating**
Power in a resistor is always positive because it depends on current squared. You must use the r.m.s. current from part (c), not the zero mean: $$P = {I_{r.m.s.}}^2 R$$ Energy is power multiplied by time: $$E = P t = {I_{r.m.s.}}^2 R t$$

Step 2: **Put in the numbers**
Use $R = 450 \Omega$ and $t = 30 \text{ ms} = 30 \times 10^{-3} \text{ s}$: $$E = (0.53)^2 \times 450 \times 30 \times 10^{-3}$$ $$E \approx 3.8 \text{ J}$$ This is the thermal energy dissipated in that short 30 ms interval.
